title: HTTP/1.1 vs. HTTP/2 vs. HTTP/3
summary: HTTP/1.1 is text, with persistent connections but one request at a time per connection.

sections.definition: HTTP/1.1 is text, with persistent connections but one request at a time per connection. HTTP/2 is binary and multiplexes many requests over a single TCP connection. HTTP/3 does the same over QUIC (UDP), which prevents one lost packet from blocking everything.
sections.analogy: 1.1: a supermarket checkout with a queue; browsers open up to 6 checkouts per store. 2: a single checkout that serves everyone by interleaving products, but if the belt jams (TCP packet loss), everyone waits. 3: each customer has their own belt within the same checkout; if one jams, the others keep going.
sections.problem: With HTTP/1.1, pages with dozens of resources suffered from the connection limit and head-of-line blocking, which led to hacks like concatenating files and sprites. HTTP/2 solved it at the HTTP level; HTTP/3 also solved it at the transport level, which matters above all on unstable mobile networks.
sections.code:wire:
# HTTP/1.1: texto legible, una petición por conexión a la vez
GET /v1/productos HTTP/1.1
Host: api.tienda.co
Connection: keep-alive

# HTTP/2: los mismos campos viajan como frames binarios en streams numerados
:method: GET   :path: /v1/productos   :authority: api.tienda.co   (stream 1)
:method: GET   :path: /v1/clientes/me (stream 3)   ← en paralelo, misma conexión
# Headers comprimidos con HPACK

# HTTP/3: igual que HTTP/2 pero sobre QUIC (UDP), TLS 1.3 integrado
Alt-Svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400   ← el servidor anuncia que soporta HTTP/3
sections.code:server:
# Uvicorn habla HTTP/1.1. HTTP/2 y HTTP/3 normalmente los maneja
# el CDN o el balanceador frente al cliente, y hacia tu app usa HTTP/1.1.
# Tu código FastAPI no cambia: la semántica (métodos, códigos, headers) es la misma.
sections.bridge:typescript: In the Network tab you can enable the Protocol column and you will see h2 or h3. The fact that today you do not need to pack everything into one giant bundle to reduce requests is partly thanks to HTTP/2 multiplexing.
sections.interview: HTTP/1.1 introduced persistent connections, but each connection serves one request at a time, so browsers open several in parallel. HTTP/2 keeps the same semantics but uses a binary format, multiplexes many requests over a single connection and compresses headers; its limitation is that it runs over TCP, and one packet loss stalls all streams. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, based on UDP, with independent streams, built-in TLS 1.3 and faster connection setup. For the backend developer the API does not change; it is usually handled by the CDN or the load balancer.
sections.myths:
• Believing HTTP/2 changes the API. The semantics are identical; the wire format changes.
  • Thinking HTTP/3 replaces TCP everywhere. It is optional and coexists with HTTP/2 as an alternative.
  • Assuming HTTP/2 completely removes head-of-line blocking. It removes it in HTTP, not in TCP.
